nodes.description: 1-deoxysphingolipids lack the C1 hydroxyl group of a canonical sphingoid base. That hydroxyl is required both for conversion into complex sphingolipids and for entry into the normal degradation route, so these metabolites accumulate rather than turning over. They are measurable in patient plasma by LC-MS, which makes this node the disease's accessible biomarker as well as its mechanism.

nodes.description: Length-dependent distal sensory loss predominantly affecting the lower limbs, spreading proximally, and often preceded by spontaneous lancinating pain. This is the presenting feature of HSAN1.

evidence.reference_title: Oral L-serine supplementation reduces production of neurotoxic deoxysphingolipids in mice and humans with hereditary sensory autonomic neuropathy type 1.
evidence.snippet: Hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathy type 1 (HSAN1) causes sensory loss that predominantly affects the lower limbs, often preceded by hyperpathia and spontaneous shooting or lancinating pain.

nodes.description: Substrate competition rather than enzyme replacement: supplying excess L-serine shifts the mutant enzyme back towards its canonical substrate and lowers 1-deoxysphingolipid production. Shown in a transgenic mouse model and in a 14-patient pilot study, and reported in HSAN1C itself in a 52-week single-patient study that titrated to 400 mg/kg/day and halved serum 1-deoxysphingolipid without demonstrating a functional benefit.

evidence.reference_title: Oral L-serine supplementation reduces production of neurotoxic deoxysphingolipids in mice and humans with hereditary sensory autonomic neuropathy type 1.
evidence.snippet: In mice bearing a transgene expressing the C133W SPTLC1 mutant linked to HSAN1, a 10% L-serine–enriched diet reduced dSL levels. L-serine supplementation also improved measures of motor and sensory performance as well as measures of male fertility.

evidence.reference_title: Oral L-serine supplementation reduces production of neurotoxic deoxysphingolipids in mice and humans with hereditary sensory autonomic neuropathy type 1.
evidence.snippet: In contrast, a 10% L-alanine–enriched diet increased dSL levels and led to severe peripheral neuropathy.

nodes.description: Serine palmitoyltransferase condenses palmitoyl-CoA with L-serine in the first and rate-limiting step of de novo sphingolipid synthesis. HSAN1 missense variants in the SPTLC1 and SPTLC2 subunits impose a permanent shift in substrate preference from L-serine towards L-alanine. The variant enzyme therefore acquires an activity the wild-type enzyme does not have, which is why the genetic context is recorded as NEOMORPHIC rather than as a loss of function.

evidence.reference_title: HSAN1 mutations in serine palmitoyltransferase reveal a close structure-function-phenotype relationship.
evidence.snippet: The mutations induce a permanent shift in the substrate preference from L-serine to L-alanine, which results in the pathological formation of atypical and neurotoxic 1-deoxy-sphingolipids (1-deoxySL).

evidence.reference_title: HSAN1 mutations in serine palmitoyltransferase reveal a close structure-function-phenotype relationship.
evidence.snippet: Despite earlier reports, canonical activity with l-serine was not reduced in any of the investigated SPT mutants.

evidence.reference_title: Mutations in the SPTLC2 subunit of serine palmitoyltransferase cause hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathy type I.
evidence.snippet: We demonstrate that these mutations result in a partial to complete loss of SPT activity in vitro and in vivo.

nodes.description: Deoxysphingoid bases are toxic to primary sensory and motor neurons, with disturbed endoplasmic-reticulum and mitochondrial calcium handling and loss of mitochondrial membrane potential as proximate cellular effects. Degeneration is length-dependent, so the longest sensory axons in the lower limbs fail first, which is why the clinical picture begins in the feet.
